answer:
**Verdict:** Hormozi would almost certainly tell you not to join an MLM to build wealth. To him it's the kind of fast-money shortcut he says keeps people poor. You'd sit at the bottom of a pay structure where someone above you controls the money, and you'd pay up front for the chance to sell something people aren't already buying.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). The vault has no statement from him about MLMs. I searched the wiki and the raw transcripts for MLM, network marketing, pyramid scheme, downline, recruiting and commission, and found nothing. Several of his main rules do apply directly, though.

**How we get there**
1. **He calls get-rich-quick thinking the reason people stay poor.** "Poor people stay poor because they want a fast way to get rich." He says the richest people he knows "pick one of these four paths, play it for a decade" ([4 paths video @ 0:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sL16tsGafcQ&t=0s)). His four paths are bootstrapping your own business, raising capital, investing and fund management. An MLM isn't one of them. It's a ready-made opportunity that you rent from someone else.
2. **He wants to be the one who gets paid first.** "You want to get paid no matter what. You want to get paid first." The top level, in his words, is "control of the money flow," like payment processors that "always get paid" ([6 Levels video @ 12:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rMJIOK_FgJk&t=758s), [@ 14:46](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rMJIOK_FgJk&t=886s)). In an MLM, the company and the people above you control the money and get paid first. You buy the starter kit and the stock before you earn anything, so you're at the bottom of the structure he ranks.
3. **He says pay follows risk, but only risk that's mispriced in your favour.** The good deals are "very risky for other people and not risky at all for them" ([@ 8:16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rMJIOK_FgJk&t=496s)). An MLM is the other way round: you carry the risk (stock, buy-ins, your time) and the company carries almost none. That's the opposite of the bet he looks for.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Sell what people already pay for.** "Find stuff people are already spending money on" ([First $100K video @ 14:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=849s)). His tests are the market and your bank statement, not a sponsor's pitch.
- **Cut costs before you take risks.** "The first step is that we have to cut all costs, so that we can take more risk" ([@ 0:32](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=32s)). Monthly buy-ins and minimum orders are the kind of cost he would cut.
- **Trust is worth more than a bigger promise.** "I would rather always sacrifice promise to gain trust" ([copywriting talk @ 13:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=789s)). Selling to friends and family using income claims spends exactly the reputation he tells people to protect.
- **Leverage means more output per unit of input** ([Diary of a CEO @ 1:45:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=6313s)). A downline gives leverage to whoever sits above you. You don't own the product, the brand or the customer list, so you can't build or sell an asset.

**What he's done instead:** He bootstrapped gyms and then licensed his own system to other gym owners (Gym Launch). That's the reverse of an MLM: he owned the system and collected from other operators, rather than paying into someone else's.

**What would change his answer:** The one part of an MLM he might value is the sales practice. He's strongly in favour of doing huge amounts of selling and copying the best people: "go Shadow the best guy and do twice the volume he's doing" ([@ 40:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=2402s)). So if it cost nothing to join, had no stock to buy, and you treated it as a few months of paid sales training rather than a wealth plan, he'd probably say the skill is real. Even then, he'd say to take the skill into a business you own.

The next point is from outside the vault: FTC and academic studies of MLM payouts find that most participants earn little or lose money. That backs up his reasoning, but it isn't something he said.

**Verdict:** No. Hormozi would keep driving a cheap car he paid cash for and put the $1M back to work. His rule is "be rich, not look rich," and a Lamborghini is something you buy to look rich.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: high). He has talked about Lamborghinis and about cars, but never about the $1M moment specifically.

**How we get there**
1. **What he said about Lamborghinis and cars.** In a copywriting video he uses the Lamborghini as an example of status bait that "might convert" a "20 year old hustle bro". He then says it's not his own taste: *"i'm all about mosy mobiles and having cash cars that you can buy for seven grand and then not have to worry about car payment so you can actually rich in your bank account rather than in other people's eyes"* ([yt-JDR-R--4HhM @ 20:31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JDR-R--4HhM&t=1231s)).
2. **The rule behind it.** Don't raise your lifestyle when your income rises, and keep spare cash so you can take risks: *"Number six, do not increase your lifestyle."* *"You want to be rich, not look rich."* ([yt-jfW6gL6hKhk @ 13:04–13:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=784s)). He says the same about cars: *"ideally a paid-off clunker is the best way to go."* (@ [2:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=128s)).
3. **Why $1M falls under that rule.** He gives the rule at the $100K stage, but his reason doesn't depend on the amount. *"you get rewarded for the risk you take on. You cannot take any risk on if you have no time and no money."* (@ [13:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=784s)). Your first $1M in profit is the stake for your next bet, and a Lamborghini turns that stake into a status symbol.

**Why he'd say it**
- Self-made wealth comes from putting your income at risk: *"most billionaires who are self-made made their money from making money."* (@ [12:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=750s))
- He spends on things that pay back: *"the day that you stop spending money on learning is the day you decide that you do not want to make more."* (@ [14:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=849s))
- In his view, wanting a status car means you still care what other people think. He calls that the thing he most wants to "beat out" of himself (see `wiki/mindset/others-opinions/caring-what-others-think.md`).

**What he's done:** His first gym paid him about $20,000 a month. He kept paying $400 a month in rent anyway and used the cash for a new location, learning and conferences ([@ 13:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=817s)).

**What would change his answer:**
- **The car is a marketing expense.** He'd likely approve if you sell to that "hustle bro" crowd and the car brings in more than it costs. That's his "spend as long as the returns hold" rule, not a personal reward.
- **You're no longer at the $1M stage.** He tells established business owners they can skip the frugality roadmap. Once the money is a rounding error next to your income, his objection gets much weaker. The vault has nothing on what he spends now that he's wealthy.

The vault's main source on this is one copywriting video. In it, he quickly mentions his own taste in cars while explaining how status works in ad copy.

**Verdict:** He'd most likely tell them to kill the free-forever plan. Users who pay nothing are users who don't value the product, and the founder needs margin before they can afford to serve the masses. He'd say to start with a paid plan and work down to cheaper tiers only when the right customers ask for one, never down to $0.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). The vault has nothing from him on freemium or free-forever SaaS plans. "free", "freemium" and "trial" turn up nothing on the topic in the wiki or the raw transcripts. The answer is built from his pricing and retention rules, which he states often.

**How we get there**
1. **The nearest case he addressed.** Skool, a SaaS product he's involved in, had cancellations over price. The fix was a cheaper paid tier, not a free one. Skool went from $99 down to $9 a month for hobbyists and kept the $99 tier for serious users. His rule: "if your ideal customer say the price is the issue, then you can add a lower tier or a standard plan. If non-ideal people say it's too expensive, just ignore it. That means that the price is actually acting as a good filter" ([yt--j8_YCWZ05Q @ 8:46](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=526s)). Even his own funnel uses a 30-day Skool trial, not a free-forever plan ([yt-jfW6gL6hKhk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk)).
2. **The rule behind it** ([thinking page](vaults/hormozi/wiki/thinking/hormozi.md), "Charge more, and sell to whoever values it most"): start expensive and work down, because "you have to make enough money to be able to serve the masses" ([yt-uWdIgftpvBI @ 0:32](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=32s)).
3. **Why free-forever falls under that rule.** It starts at the bottom, with zero margin, and takes away the filter that price provides. You end up with the users who value the product least, while the founder pays for their hosting and support.

**Why he'd say it**
- **A higher price brings better customers.** "if you raise your price, you increase the emotional investment, you increase the perceived value, you increase the results, and you decrease the demandingness of the customer." ([yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4 @ 7:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=453s)) Free users are the reverse on every count.
- **Founders undercharge out of fear.** "they're so afraid of charging money that they actually sell themselves out of a sale" (same source, @ 7:33)
- **The business has to cover the cost of each customer.** "fundamentally all businesses have the cost of getting customers and what you make from those customers as the core economic arbitrage that makes a business a business" ([yt-uWdIgftpvBI @ 0:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uWdIgftpvBI&t=0s)). A free-forever user costs money to acquire and serve, and pays nothing back unless they upgrade. His fix for expensive customers is to "make more from each one." ([yt-tGhe3sBuk34 @ 8:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=530s))
- **Customers who pay up front are better customers.** On annual plans he says buyers are "more qualified because they've paid more up front" ([yt--j8_YCWZ05Q @ 15:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=952s)).
- **Avoid the middle.** "either sell extremely expensive stuff to a select few or sell something super cheap to everyone. The middle is where people die." (yt-uWdIgftpvBI @ 0:00) Even "super cheap to everyone" is a paid price.

**What he's done:** He does give things away, but only content: "we'll put everything out there uh for free so no pay walls" ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 2:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=137s)). He's open that this content brings him deal flow. Free is how he gets attention. It isn't his product.

**What would change his answer:** If the free plan works like his free content, as a cheap way to attract people that measurably turns into paying ideal customers, he might accept it as marketing. He'd judge it on whether the money from paying customers covers the cost of the free ones, the same way he judges ad spend. A free plan kept because the founder is afraid to charge would still get the verdict above. The inference could also break because his pricing examples are mostly services (gyms, HVAC, coaching), where each extra customer costs real money to serve. In SaaS, an extra user costs close to nothing, and he never addresses that difference in the vault.

My own view, separately: freemium works for some products where users spread the product to others, which is a case his rules don't cover.

**Verdict:** Only if the friend is the best person he could get for the job and passes the same screen as anyone else. Hormozi would not hire someone because they're his best friend. He picks people for how good they are and whether they fit his values, and he warns that the people close to you won't give you honest feedback.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: **low–medium**). The vault never covers hiring friends or what a first hire should look like, so this comes from close cases and his general rules.

**How we get there**
1. **The closest case is how he recruited Leila, and it was about skill.** On their first date he pitched her on working for him because she was good at the job: "I pitched her on working for me I was like quit your job work for me… she was a a personal trainer I had a bunch of gyms and I was like if you're this good you should totally work for me" ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 17:29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=1049s)). This was competence first, from someone he'd just met. It wasn't loyalty.
2. **He screens every hire hard and wants mismatches out early.** "on the screening Parts on the front end we're like these are the values we have here" and "if your worldview is contrary to this then you shouldn't work here" (yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 1:16:08, 1:16:40). He also says a hire who fakes a fit will "get fired quickly". With a best friend, that firing costs you the friendship too.
3. **He says friends and family won't tell you the truth.** "people want to protect your feelings, your friends, your family, they don't want you to feel bad. The market does not care" ([yt-XGm2ERU9qtA @ 15:41](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=941s)). A first employee who is also your best friend sits right in the zone of softened feedback he warns about.
4. **The friend gets no pass for being close.** He lost everything when he went into business with a partner he already knew had been indicted for fraud: "I knew this getting... into business with him" (yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 19:06). That man was a business partner, not a friend or an employee, so this only shows that he now regrets relaxing his judgment for a convenient relationship.

So: run the friend through the values screen and the 4:59 scenario question like any other candidate. Hire them if they'd be your pick among strangers. Otherwise don't.

**What would change his answer:** if the friend has a proven track record in the exact role, step 1 applies and he'd hire them happily. Leila shows he has no problem mixing a close relationship with work when the person is excellent. One thing points slightly the other way. He cites a finding that employees with a friend outside work "stay five times longer" ([yt--j8_YCWZ05Q @ 16:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=1018s)). The vault marks that as research he passed on, not his own view, and it's about retention, not first hires.

Want me to save this as a file in `derived/`?

**Verdict:** He'd have the owner drop "first month free." It gives away the month when most members quit and attracts people who weren't going to pay. He'd tell them to charge money up front, ideally for an annual plan, and to build a plan for getting new members through their first month and past day 90.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). The vault has no statement from him about free trials or "first month free." The answer comes from his rules on churn, pricing and money models. Strictly, it rests on one close source, his 2026 retention talk, plus his pricing rule from a 2026 consult, so it's at the high end of medium.

**How we get there**
1. **The nearest case he covered:** the first month of a membership. He says month one has the most cancellations: "have a very specific strategy for getting people past the first month cuz that's the biggest month of churn" ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 4:57, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=297s). Churn then "drops to around 10% or less" after day 90 (@ 3:53).
2. **The rules behind it** ([[thinking/hormozi]]):
   - Charge more and sell to whoever values it most.
   - Pull cash forward.
   - Let price act as a filter.
   - Get people past day 90.
3. **Applying them:** "first month free" breaks all four. It collects no cash in the highest-churn month. It brings in the members price would have screened out. And the first decision to pay comes at day 30, right when people are most likely to leave.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Free brings in the wrong members.** He says price is a filter: "If non-ideal people say it's too expensive, just ignore it. That means that the price is actually acting as a good filter" (@ 8:46). A free month removes that filter.
- **A higher price can mean better members, not fewer.** "if you raise your price, you increase the emotional investment, you increase the perceived value, you increase the results, and you decrease the demandingness of the customer." ([[yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4]] @ 7:33, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=453s). He also says owners "are so afraid of charging money that they actually sell themselves out of a sale" (@ 7:33). Giving the month away is a version of that fear.
- **He wants cash early, not late.** A money model is about "how do you pull cash forward accelerate cash conversion uh within a business so that you can scale" ([[yt-tGhe3sBuk34]] @ 8:17, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGhe3sBuk34&t=497s). A free first month pushes cash back. If leads cost too much, his advice is "make more from each one" (@ 8:50), not charge them less.
- **Sell annual plans instead.** "annual always has lower churn than monthly and it's because you only need to decide one time rather than 12", and "they're also more qualified because they've paid more up front" ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 15:52). He says any recurring business should have an annual plan "like today" (@ 16:26). He suggests a discount of about 16–17%, "buy 10 get two" (@ 15:52). That's a discount for paying up front, the opposite of a free month.
- **Fix the first month with onboarding, not a lower price.** "pin the fast win up front so new members hit that value ideally within the first 24 hours" (@ 13:06). For a gym, that means a booked first session, a coach who knows the new member's name, and early results they can see.

**What he's done:** He ran gyms himself and later licensed his gym system to other owners as Gym Launch ([[yt-x3e73Qn6NOo]], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo). The vault has no record of him running a free-month promotion. Gym Launch is widely known for paid six-week challenges, but that comes from outside the vault.

**What would change his answer:** The free month would have to work as an entry offer that pays for itself. That means the numbers show free signups turning into paid (better still, annual) members at a rate that beats a paid front-end offer, while the gym stays break-even or better on acquisition. He decides on evidence, not taste. If the owner's join-versus-cancel numbers showed the free month winning, he'd keep it, because "the offer's already converting, so I don't really want to mess with that." ([[yt-MH-IMJxbUY4]] @ 24:06, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=1446s).

A caveat on the sources: his retention numbers are Skool platform averages, and Skool is a company he's involved with. He says the numbers fit online and consumer subscriptions, and a gym is close to that but not the same.

**Verdict:** He'd tell you not to do it. A crypto day-trading course is the "fast way to get rich" he says keeps people poor, and putting your savings into it spends the cushion that's meant to let you take a real risk later.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: high). The vault has nothing from him on crypto or day trading specifically (I searched the wiki and the raw transcripts). But several of his rules, each repeated across more than one source, apply directly.

**How we get there**
1. The nearest case is shortcuts. He says "Poor people stay poor because they want a fast way to get rich." His alternative is to pick one of four paths (bootstrap, raise money, invest, manage a fund) and stick with it for ten years: "the richest people that I know pick one of these four paths, play it for a decade, and then end up with more money than everyone else that is just chasing shortcuts." ([yt-sL16tsGafcQ @ 0:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sL16tsGafcQ&t=0s))
2. The rule behind it, from his thinking page: he wants compounding over a long time, he's against chasing "the next shiny opportunity," and he puts safety first so you can afford risk later.
3. Day trading crypto fails all three. It's short-term by design, it's the textbook shiny opportunity, and it spends the savings that are supposed to buy you room to take risks.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Savings are what let you take risk, not the thing you gamble.** "The first step is that we have to cut all costs, so that we can take more risk." ([yt-jfW6gL6hKhk @ 0:32](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=32s)) "You cannot take any risk on if you have no time and no money." (same video @ 13:04) He says he felt wealthiest at $100K in the bank, because "that was when I stopped having to worry about tomorrow" (@ 0:00).
- **Money comes from active income, not from trading your stack.** "There are only four ways to get money. Steal, inherit, marry into it, trade for it." He means trading value with customers ([yt-rMJIOK_FgJk @ 0:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rMJIOK_FgJk&t=0s)). Even on investing, his slowest path, he says "almost no one makes their money this way. They have already have a high active income and then they begin investing." ([yt-sL16tsGafcQ @ 14:12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sL16tsGafcQ&t=852s))
- **Don't bet on what you don't know. Sell what people already pay for.** "the best way to look is not to risk it on something that you don't know, but find stuff people are already spending money on." ([yt-jfW6gL6hKhk @ 14:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=849s))
- **Get your oxygen mask on first.** "get yourself out of the hole as fast as humanly possible." ([yt-XGm2ERU9qtA @ 17:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=1073s))

**The nuance he'd add:** he does want you to pay for learning. He names "implementation help (courses, communities, and especially one-on-one tutoring)" as one of three places your savings should go, and says "the day that you stop spending money on learning is the day you decide that you do not want to make more." ([yt-jfW6gL6hKhk @ 11:25 and 14:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=685s)) But he calls these "minor investments," and they go toward a skill people will pay you for. So a modest course in sales, copywriting or ads that leads to income fits his advice. Your whole savings on a course for trading those savings doesn't.

**What would change his answer:** if you already had a high active income and a funded cushion, and this were a small, capped amount you could lose entirely, he'd treat it as a small bet rather than a mistake. Even then it wouldn't be one of his four paths to wealth.

My own note: his advice here lines up with mainstream personal-finance advice, so I don't disagree with it.

**Verdict:** No. Hormozi would not recommend a 4-day week as a way to run or grow a 10-person agency. He would first ask what's limiting the business. If the agency is short of delivery capacity, cutting a day makes that limit worse. If it's short of clients, a shorter week doesn't get it more. He would also not call a 4-day week wrong. He says there's no single right way to run a company. He would just never build one himself, and he'd tell you to be upfront about whichever culture you choose.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: medium). He has never talked about a 4-day week. This answer applies his rules on finding the constraint, hiring for high performance, and how hard people should work.

**How we get there**
1. **He starts every business problem by finding the constraint.** "the first problem I try to delineate is this is a supply constraint business or a demand constraint business." ([yt-OQf2Ba-Lp_4 @ 3:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OQf2Ba-Lp_4&t=227s)). He warns that owners often "fix a problem that's already a problem that if you fix it, makes your existing problem worse." (@ 4:19). An agency usually sells hours of its people's time. Removing 20% of those hours shrinks supply directly, unless output per hour rises enough to make up for it.
2. **His culture rule is to set expectations, not pick one correct schedule.** His companies "try to maintain a culture of high performance" and screen for it at hiring. For example, they ask candidates what they would do if a 30-minute question came in at 4:59 and their shift ended at 5 ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 1:16:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=4568s)). He also says "I just I just hardcore reject there is a right way to do things" (@ 1:17:13), and that if your worldview is different "you shouldn't work here because there's... another company that totally shares your worldview" (@ 1:16:40). So he wouldn't tell you a 4-day agency is immoral. His point is that the owner has to choose a culture and state it clearly.
3. **His own view on hours points the other way.** "I work all the time" ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 1:09:28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=4168s)). Since 2025 he goes further: "if you're under 30 and you have no responsibilities, I recommend working as many hours per week as humanly possible" ([yt-XGm2ERU9qtA @ 11:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=712s)). Taken together, the "more output per hour" case for a 4-day week is one he'd only accept if the numbers prove it.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Fewer days doesn't mean doing less work.** When he says "do less", he means doing fewer things, not working fewer hours: "focus is achieved not through addition, but subtraction" ([yt-jfW6gL6hKhk @ 4:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=258s)). He also says "I promise your team's 10 times more overwhelmed" when it has too many priorities ([yt--JLN1d1ZKUU @ 13:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=794s)). For an overloaded team, his fix is to cut projects, cut meetings and protect blocks of uninterrupted time. Shortening the week isn't it.
- **He judges by output.** "if you do not know the inputs that are going to get the output that you want then what are you doing" ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo @ 38:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=2338s)). If someone said "we'll get the same output in 4 days", he'd ask for proof from a test, not belief.

**What would change his answer:**
- The agency is short of clients rather than capacity, and it runs a test showing output and client results hold with 4 days.
- The 4-day week is used deliberately as a hiring advantage, to recruit better people than competitors can. That uses his rule of treating recruits as a market you sell to.

In either case he'd say: fine, but write it into the expectations from the first interview.

*My own view:* his rules come from high-growth, owner-run companies. A 10-person agency that cares more about keeping staff than growing fast may reasonably weigh this differently. I can save this answer to `derived/` if you want to keep it.

**Verdict:** He'd tell the coach to cut to one product, sold to one avatar on one channel, until it makes $1 million. Twelve products at once breaks his 1-1-1 rule. It also spreads a small operation across 12 bets, so none of them gets good, and it overwhelms the customers it does land.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (confidence: high). He states the rule directly in one source. The ideas behind it (focus, subtraction, and overwhelm as a reason customers cancel) appear in four. He never discussed a coach with exactly 12 products.

**How we get there**
1. The closest thing he said: "you want to sell one product or service to one avatar on one channel until you make $1 million." ([[yt-jfW6gL6hKhk]] @ 8:09, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=489s)
2. The rule behind it, from his thinking page: do one thing, and remove things until it gets better ([[thinking/hormozi]]).
3. Twelve products at the same time is the opposite of that. The 1-1-1 rule is aimed at people under $1M, which describes most solo coaches. So he'd apply it as it stands.

**Why he'd say it**
- **Too many things means none of them gets good.** "The price of wanting to be good at everything is being good at nothing." He adds: "Nobody wants a thing that has everything." ([[yt-XGm2ERU9qtA]] @ 22:24, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XGm2ERU9qtA&t=1344s)
- **You can't go deep on 12 things.** "you can't go deep if you have too many things" ([[yt--JLN1d1ZKUU]] @ 8:49, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=529s). His test for a business is "If we only did this one thing, would we accomplish all of our goals?" (@ 3:20)
- **It hurts customers too.** "The number one reason people churn, outside of price, is overwhelm." ([[yt--j8_YCWZ05Q]] @ 9:18, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-j8_YCWZ05Q&t=558s)
- **Several products often means fear, not strategy.** "when people are afraid of making decisions, they say yes to everything because they're so afraid of saying no" ([[yt-XGm2ERU9qtA]] @ 22:58)
- **Spreading bets lowers the upside.** "you have one real bet that you can make on it. And so it's like you want to make that bet worth it." ([[yt--JLN1d1ZKUU]] @ 10:27)

**What he's done:** In his Skool Games community, overwhelm was the top reason people cancelled. He responded by removing things: he cut the calls from three a week to one and moved the big download from monthly to quarterly ([[yt--JLN1d1ZKUU]] @ 11:35). He also admits he struggles with focus himself. He says he gets impatient after about 30 days and starts a second approach, and calls that a mistake.

**What would change his answer:** He doesn't object to a business having more than one price. He tells every business to list a premium tier about 10x the main price. He also likes a menu upsell, where a customer chooses between two options after the first sale. His words: "Getting the first sale is the hard part" ([[yt-o64cI6tebnU]] @ 7:06). So one core offer with a premium tier, a cheaper downsell and a follow-on upsell, all for the same customer, would get his approval. What breaks his rules is 12 separate products, each needing its own marketing and its own buyers. Once the core offer passes $1M, he'd be fine with adding more.
